competitors.price: Individual $6/mo or $60/yr — custom domain INCLUDED at this entry personal tier (effective $5/mo annual). Duo $10/mo ($96/yr), Family $14/mo ($132/yr). Business: Basic $4/user/mo (NO custom domain), Standard $6/user/mo (custom domains, up to 100), Professional $10/user/mo. 30-day free trial, no card.
competitors.positioning: The mainstream "privacy-respecting, ad-free Gmail replacement" for individuals and small teams, built on open standards (JMAP/IMAP) with best-in-class custom-domain and alias management — practical privacy rather than end-to-end encryption.
competitors.notes: Healthy, independent (employee-owned since 2013 Opera buyback; operating since 1999) — no shutdown risk signals. Privacy caveats Letters can attack: NO end-to-end encryption (Fastmail can read stored mail; at-rest server encryption only), Australian jurisdiction under the 2018 Assistance and Access anti-encryption Act (publicly acknowledged losing customers over it), mail stored in US (NYC) — Five Eyes at both ends; but no ads, no ad-surveillance scanning, strong advocacy record, Masked Email. Custom domain is NOT price-gated for consumers: every personal plan from $6/mo Individual includes up to 100 domains, catch-all, unlimited own-domain aliases — undercuts Letters' $8/mailbox and $20/creator-domain on price. Creator gap Letters can own: Fastmail is a mailbox, not a creator platform — ToS bans bulk/duplicative sending (accounts closed for it), send caps ~4,000-16,000 msgs/day by tier (120/day on trial), no newsletter, subscriber, or audience tooling; indie authors must bolt on Buttondown/Ghost/etc. Deliverability: long-tenured, well-managed shared sending infrastructure with guided SPF/DKIM/DMARC for custom domains and participation in sender-certification ecosystems; solid 1:1 reputation, but shared IPs and no bulk sending. No major privacy/breach incidents found 2025-2026.

competitors.price: Free tier $0 (no custom domain). Entry paid: Mail Plus $3.99/mo billed annually ($4.99 month-to-month) — the first tier that includes a custom domain (1 domain, 10 addresses, 15 GB). Proton Unlimited $9.99/mo annual ($12.99 monthly) adds 3 custom domains + VPN/Pass/500 GB. Duo $14.99/mo, Family $29.99/mo (3 domains). Business: Mail Essentials ~$7.99/user/mo, Mail Professional ~$10.99/user/mo, Business Suite ~$13.99/user/mo (annual billing); frequent promos cut 30-50%.
competitors.positioning: Swiss privacy-tech suite selling zero-access encrypted email (bundled with VPN, Drive, Pass, Calendar) to privacy-conscious consumers and SMBs as the mainstream alternative to Gmail/Outlook surveillance business models.
competitors.notes: Healthy, growing vendor (~100M+ accounts; nonprofit-foundation-controlled) — the default migration destination for Skiff refugees, and the incumbent Letters must differentiate against on privacy email. Key facts for positioning: (1) Custom domain is cheap but capped — $3.99/mo gets 1 domain vs Letters' $20 creator-domain; Proton undercuts on price but sells a mailbox, not a creator identity product. (2) Not a newsletter platform: ToS prohibits bulk mail; paid plans limited to ~300 msgs/hour / ~1,000/day, 100 recipients/message, reputation-throttled — indie creators still need Buttondown/Ghost/beehiiv for sending, so Letters can position as creator-complete where Proton is send-limited. (3) Privacy record is strong technically (zero-access/E2E, open-source clients, audited, no ads) but compelance incidents dent the halo: 2021 French climate-activist IP logging (Proton scrubbed 'no IP logs' claim), May 2024 Spanish case where a recovery email led to de-anonymization via Apple, and compliance with 8,313 of 9,301 Swiss legal orders in 2025 (10,368 of 11,023 in 2024). (4) Jurisdiction in flux: Aug 2025 Proton began relocating infrastructure out of Switzerland (Lumo AI to Germany first) over the proposed OSCPT surveillance ordinance (ID collection + 6-month metadata retention for services >5,000 users); CEO Andy Yen has threatened full exit. Encrypted-mailbox UX also has creator friction: E2E only works Proton-to-Proton, no IMAP without Bridge (paid, desktop-only). No shutdown/acquisition risk signals.

competitors.price: $99/yr (~$8.25/mo) HEY for You, @hey.com address only, annual billing only; custom domain requires HEY for Work/Domains at $12/user/mo (first user $10/mo), billed monthly — ~$120-144/yr solo; HEY for Families $179/yr (5 people); vanity 3-char $349/yr, 2-char $999/yr
competitors.positioning: Opinionated premium email-plus-calendar from 37signals that replaces the inbox paradigm (Screener, Imbox, tracker-blocking) on a paid no-ads model, with custom domains sold as a separate business-priced tier rather than part of the personal product.
competitors.notes: Privacy: blocks spy pixels by default and names the tracking vendor (industry-leading; prompted Apple Mail Privacy Protection), no ads/no data sale, incentives aligned by paid model — but NOT end-to-end/zero-access encrypted (unlike Proton/Tuta), US-based, and mail lives in a proprietary system (no IMAP/POP; MBOX export and lifetime post-cancellation forwarding after first paid year mitigate lock-in). Custom domain: fully functional (send/receive/forwarding, solo use allowed) but gated behind the $12/user/mo Work/Domains tier — a solo author pays ~45% more than HEY for You and 6x Letters' $20/creator-domain positioning at the entry point. Creator angle: HEY World is a real differentiator (email world@hey.com to publish a tracker-free blog with email subscribers) but publishes on world.hey.com, not the creator's own domain — identity remains hey.com-first, which is Letters' opening. Deliverability: no notable complaints found; mature self-run infrastructure (completed cloud/S3 exit June 2025, 18PB own storage across two data centers); company is profitable and self-funded — negligible shutdown risk. Brand risk: DHH/Basecamp 2021 politics controversy and DHH's continuing polarizing persona alienates a slice of the indie-creator demographic; conversely his anti-surveillance stance attracts another slice. Annual-only billing on personal plan; 30-day free trial; no AI-training-on-mail concerns reported.

competitors.price: DEFUNCT — nothing purchasable in 2025-2026. Legacy pricing (2023): Free tier with 10GB; Essentials $3/mo, Pro $8/mo, Business $12/mo (annual billing). Custom domains were included on ALL tiers including free (from mid-2023), with domain registration via Skiff from ~$2 first year.
competitors.positioning: Skiff was the closest historical analog to Letters — a privacy-first, end-to-end-encrypted email + docs/calendar/drive suite with free custom domains and an 'own your email' pitch (~2M users) — until Notion acquired it in February 2024 and shut it down.
competitors.notes: DEFUNCT: Acquired by Notion 2024-02-09; all services (Mail, Pages, Calendar, Drive) sunset 2024-08-09 after a ~6-month export window; email forwarding only continued through 2025-02-09. No automatic migration — users had to manually export (MBOX/EML, contacts, calendar, custom-domain DNS re-pointing). Migration destinations that published Skiff-specific guides: Proton Mail, Tuta, StartMail, Mailfence, mailbox.org. The Skiff team built Notion Mail (launched April 2025), but it was a Gmail client with AI — not private, not E2EE, no custom-domain hosting — and Notion announced Notion Mail itself shuts down 2026-09-22. SCORING BASIS (what users lost): Privacy 3 — genuinely E2EE with source-available clients, no ads/trackers, but documented failures (Sonar-reported XSS enabling decrypted-email theft; remote content loading ON by default; no DNSSEC/DANE; TLS 1.0 accepted; DMARC quarantine-not-reject; no outbound MTA-STS) and the ultimate privacy failure: acquisition + shutdown broke the ownership promise. Custom domain 4 — best-in-class gating while alive (free on every tier), docked because the hosting evaporated and domains went dark on the platform. Creator UX 3 — polished modern apps and generous free tier, but no newsletter/creator tooling and now zero continuity. Deliverability 2 — generous free tier attracted spammers/phishers; user reports of mail landing in spam (HN); DMARC/MTA-STS misconfigurations documented. COMPETITIVE TAKEAWAY FOR LETTERS: Skiff's ~2M orphaned users are the exact 'burned by a shuttered privacy-email startup' audience — Letters' $8/mailbox / $20/creator-domain must answer the longevity/exit-risk objection Skiff created (data export guarantees, domain portability), since 'free custom domains forever' proved unsustainable.

competitors.price: Business Starter $7/user/mo annual ($8.40 flexible) — custom domain Gmail included at this entry tier; Business Standard $14 ($16.80 flexible); Business Plus $22 ($26.40 flexible); Enterprise custom. Prices rose ~$2/user in Jan 2025 when Gemini AI was bundled in (Starter $6→$7, Standard $12→$14).
competitors.positioning: The incumbent all-in-one business suite: custom-domain Gmail bundled with Drive/Docs/Meet/Calendar and now-mandatory Gemini AI, priced per user with a 300-user cap on Business tiers.
competitors.notes: PRIVACY (2/5): Google states it does not scan Workspace content for ads, but the surrounding reputation is poor for a privacy-first audience: 2025 brought sustained backlash over Gemini/smart-features processing of inbox content (settings split across two places, both must be disabled; disabling breaks basic features), a Nov 2025 Illinois class-action over Gemini access to Gmail content, and criticism of mandatory Gemini bundling with no opt-out pricing. No E2EE; client-side encryption is gated to higher/Enterprise tiers. Google remains an advertising company at the account level. CUSTOM DOMAIN (5/5): included on every paid tier including the cheapest; mature multi-domain/alias support — but self-service DNS (MX/SPF/DKIM/DMARC) setup, which non-technical authors find intimidating. CREATOR UX (3/5): familiar Gmail interface is a plus, but it is a generic business suite with an admin console that is overkill for a solo author; no newsletter/audience features; ~2,000 external recipients/day sending cap forces creators onto a separate ESP for their list. DELIVERABILITY (4/5): shared Google infrastructure is near best-in-class for 1:1 correspondence, but 2025 B2B benchmarks show Workspace inbox placement fell ~10.5 percentage points as Google tightened filtering, and safe-send guidance for new domains is only ~20-30 emails/day during warmup. LETTERS ANGLE: at $8/mailbox Letters is price-comparable to Starter ($7) while leading on privacy and creator-specific UX; Google wins on ecosystem breadth (Drive/Docs/Meet) and brand trust in deliverability. Not defunct; no shutdown risk.

competitors.price: Free (1 domain, 25 aliases, 500 forwards/day, receive-only); Premium $9/mo ($108/yr) is the tier that unlocks sending FROM your custom domain via SMTP (6,000 sends/mo, 30 domains, 100 aliases/domain); Business $24/mo (30,000 sends/mo, 100 domains); a low-profile Light plan ~$50/yr exists. Custom-domain receiving/forwarding is free; custom-domain sending is gated at $9/mo.
competitors.positioning: Lightweight custom-domain email forwarding — aliases on your own domain relayed into the inbox you already have (usually Gmail) — positioned as the 5-minute, $0-9/mo on-ramp to a professional address rather than actual mailbox hosting.
competitors.notes: Not a Letters substitute but a cheap partial alternative: no mailboxes, storage, or webmail — creators still need Gmail/another inbox, so the surveillance problem Letters solves remains (key wedge). Privacy hygiene is genuinely decent: pledges never to log email content, delivered mail purged near-instantly, failed mail retained max 7 days, configurable logging levels, GDPR-compliant with EU data in French OVH datacenters, 72h breach-notification policy, no known breaches — but it is a plaintext relay, not encrypted hosting. Deliverability is well regarded (custom SRS envelope rewriting, <5s average forward, 99.99% SLA claim, 30M+ emails/month, 200K+ users), though forwarded mail to Gmail still spam-folders often enough to be a recurring support topic, and SMTP send caps (6K/mo on $9 Premium) rule out newsletter sending. Ownership churn: founded 2013, bought for $5K in 2017 by Antoine Minoux and Cyril Nicodeme, grown to $350K+ ARR, then sold to first-time solo acquirer Matthew Tse (announced early 2025) — a continuity/trust question for anyone putting their author identity on it. Creator fit: excellent for hello@smallpress.com forwarding on a budget; weak for creators wanting a real private inbox, sent-mail archive, or newsletter workflows. Letters' $8/mailbox undercuts Premium ($9) while delivering actual hosting.

competitors.price: Free: $0 (3,000 emails/mo, 100/day cap, 1 custom domain — custom domain is NOT price-gated); Pro $20/mo (50,000 emails, 10 domains, +$20/mo per extra domain block); Scale from $90/mo (100k emails, 1,000 domains) to $1,150/mo (2.5M); Broadcasts/marketing billed per contact: free to 1,000 contacts, then $40/mo per 5,000 contacts up to $650/mo per 150,000
competitors.positioning: Developer-first transactional email API (built by the creator of React Email) with a bare-bones contact-priced Broadcasts add-on — it sells sending infrastructure to developers, not mailbox hosting or a creator suite.
competitors.notes: Category mismatch is the decision-relevant fact: Resend is a SENDING API, not email hosting — no mailboxes, no inbox UX on the creator's domain (inbound email parsing launched 2025 but is API-level receive for apps, not a hosted inbox), so it complements rather than substitutes Letters' $8/mailbox offer; it competes only with Letters' outbound/newsletter story. Custom sending domains are ungated (1 free, 10 on Pro $20/mo, 1,000 on Scale) with a clean DNS/DKIM flow — strong on that axis but sending-only, hence 4 not 5. Privacy: SOC 2 Type II, GDPR/DPA, AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.3, annual pentests, no ad-surveillance business model, but open/click tracking is a product feature, content transits US AWS infrastructure, and the Feb 21 2024 incident (an engineer's local migration dropped ALL production tables → ~12h full outage, ~5 min permanent data loss) shows operational immaturity; a second outage Nov 18 2025 (~3h, upstream Cloudflare) took down sending. Deliverability: generally well-regarded modern stack, metrics dashboard, recommends <0.08% complaint rate, $3M invested in email-safety systems, dedicated IPs available — but default shared IP pools on a hyper-growth self-serve dev platform carry inherited-reputation risk and there is no long enterprise track record (founded 2023). Creator UX is the weak flank: everything assumes a developer (API keys, React Email templates); Broadcasts is a minimal editor, and $40/mo at 5,001 contacts is expensive next to creator newsletter tools. Company is healthy, not defunct: $21.5M raised ($18M round Dec 2024), ~$25M revenue in 2025 (+400%), acquired Briefer and Mergent. Versus Letters: Resend cannot answer 'privacy-first hosted mailbox on my domain, no surveillance' — the threat is only that a technical creator pairs free/cheap Resend sending with any mailbox provider.

competitors.price: Free (100 subscribers, includes custom sending domain + API); Basic $9/mo (1,000 subs, removes branding); Standard $29/mo (5,000 subs, automations, surveys, and the tier that gates custom HOSTING domain for archives/subscribe pages); Professional $79/mo (10k-25k subs, dedicated IP, white-labeling). Custom sending domain is free on ALL tiers; custom hosting domain requires Standard $29/mo. Pricing scales with subscriber count. 0% platform fee on paid subscriptions (Stripe fees only).
competitors.positioning: Minimalist, privacy-respecting newsletter platform for indie writers and developers — deliberately small, founder-run, positioned as the anti-Mailchimp/anti-Substack with markdown-first UX and no cut of subscription revenue.
competitors.notes: IMPORTANT scope distinction for Letters: Buttondown is newsletter SENDING only — it provides no mailbox/inbox hosting, so it does not compete with Letters' $8/mailbox offer; overlap is on the $20/creator-domain newsletter-identity axis. Privacy: privacy-by-design, GDPR-compliant, tracking pixels can be fully disabled, no data used for advertising — but not a zero-tracking product by default (open/click tracking exists as a feature), hence 4 not 5. Deliverability: reviews cite ~98% inbox placement, SPF/DKIM/DMARC handled, small clean IP pool, dedicated IP at $79 tier; several minor availability incidents in 2025-2026 (API outage Nov 2025, tracked links May 2026, broken images Jun 2026, 25-min api.buttondown.email DNS outage Jul 2026 during Heroku-to-AWS migration) — all with public postmortems, a transparency positive. Company: ~6 employees, bootstrapped, $392K revenue 2024 (up from $180K in 2023), founder Justin Duke (affiliated with Third South Capital) personally answers support; GetLatka reports an M&A offer in April 2025 — not defunct, but tiny-team concentration risk. Jan 2025 pricing update moved automations down to $29/mo and made API access free — prices moved down, not up. Custom-domain scoring rationale: sending domain free on every tier (generous) but hosted-archive custom domain gated at $29/mo (vs Letters' $20 creator-domain), hence 4. Some third-party reviews disagree on Professional tier cap (10k vs 25k subscribers) — treat that number as approximate.

competitors.price: Free to publish; 10% of paid-subscription revenue forever plus Stripe fees (~2.9% + $0.30 + 0.7% billing; ~$0.95 taken from a $5/mo sub). Custom WEB domain: one-time $50 per publication, available at every tier (no monthly gating) plus your own ~$15/yr registration. Custom-domain EMAIL: not offered at any price — mail always sends from [publication]@substack.com.
competitors.positioning: Substack is the network-effect subscription-newsletter/media platform for independent writers — free to start, monetized via a perpetual 10% revenue share, with built-in recommendations-driven audience growth and, since 2025-26, native advertising.
competitors.notes: Not an email host — a publishing platform; the overlap with Letters is identity and audience ownership. Key wedges: (1) custom domain is website-only; the From address is permanently @substack.com and cannot be changed (only reply-to forwarding), so creators never own their sending identity; (2) privacy record is weak — 40/100 (grade C) in a 2026 audit, tracks opens/clicks/reading time, ignores Do Not Track, shares data with analytics/ad partners, and an Oct 2025 API-scraping breach exposed ~697,313 records (names, emails, phone numbers, Stripe IDs, bios) that Substack only disclosed Feb 5, 2026; (3) after a $100M Series C (Jul 2025, $1.1B valuation) it piloted native ads Dec 2025 and launched 'native sponsorships' Jun 2026, reversing its founding anti-ad mission — a surveillance-trajectory signal Letters can position against; (4) deliverability rides substack.com's strong shared reputation (Gmail trusts it), but that reputation is non-portable: exporting subscribers means restarting from zero, an explicit lock-in; heavy Promotions-tab placement and Gmail's Sept 2025 engagement-based ranking hurt low-engagement lists. Creator economics: excellent free on-ramp and best-in-class discovery network, but the 10% cut (plus ~3.6% processing) compounds forever vs Letters' flat $20/creator-domain. Privacy score 2 not 1 because passwords/card data were not breached and data isn't sold outright; custom_domain 2 not 1 because the $50 web-domain option exists ungated; deliverability 4 reflects strong shared reputation minus Promotions-tab and lock-in caveats.

competitors.price: Micro $19/yr (~$1.60/mo); Mini $9/mo ($90/yr); Standard $29/mo ($290/yr); Maxi $99/mo ($990/yr). Custom domains (unlimited, with unlimited mailboxes/aliases) are included at EVERY tier, even $19/yr Micro — pricing is by usage (storage + daily message volume), not per mailbox or per domain.
competitors.positioning: Swiss no-nonsense, pay-for-usage email hosting for unlimited custom domains and mailboxes at a flat price, aimed at individuals, developers, and small teams who want standards-based (IMAP/SMTP) correspondence email without a productivity suite.
competitors.notes: Alive and stable (no shutdown/acquisition risk signals; small Swiss company, Migadu Mail GmbH). Key facts: (1) Free plan discontinued; cheapest tier is now Micro $19/yr with 5GB pooled storage, ~25-mailbox soft cap, and account-wide limits of 200 incoming / 20 outgoing per day (Mini: 1,000/100; Standard: 3,000/500; Maxi: 10,000/2,000). All limits are pooled across every mailbox on the account. (2) ToS explicitly prohibits newsletters, bulk, automated, and transactional email — combined with daily send caps this makes Migadu structurally unable to serve newsletter writers; it only covers the identity-mailbox half of the indie-creator job. (3) Privacy reputation is strong and unusually honest (no ads/tracking/data mining, Swiss law, TLS + operator-side at-rest encryption) but there is no zero-access/E2E encryption — the operator can technically read mail; no known privacy incidents. (4) Deliverability is adequate for low-volume correspondence (individually verified customers, low volume keeps IP reputation decent) but there are documented complaints of Outlook spam-foldering Migadu mail, weak inbound spam filtering, and occasional 1hr+ outages (~two nines on MX per one long-term review). (5) UX is admin-panel-first with a basic 'usable' webmail; setup requires DNS literacy. Competitive read vs Letters: Migadu massively undercuts Letters on identity email ($19/yr unlimited domains vs $20/mo per creator-domain) — Letters should not compete on mailbox price; its defensible wedge is exactly what Migadu bans and lacks: newsletter/audience sending on the creator's domain plus polished indie-creator UX.

competitors.price: EUR 1/month (~$1.05) flat for everything; NO tier includes custom domain at any price (unsupported by design). Includes 2GB storage (reportedly doubled to 4GB free in Feb 2026) and 2 aliases (some sources: 3); extra storage EUR 0.25/GB/mo up to 20GB, extra aliases EUR 0.10/mo each; anonymous cash payment accepted.
competitors.positioning: German green-energy privacy mailbox at EUR 1/month — anonymous, encrypted, ad-free personal email that deliberately refuses custom domains to avoid storing any unencrypted user-identity data.
competitors.notes: Active and healthy (independent, self-funded, operating since 2009) — not defunct. Custom domains are rejected on principle: Posteo says mapping a domain to a user would require storing unencrypted identity data; only workaround is outbound-only SMTP relay with a foreign From (no inbound, breaks DKIM/DMARC alignment). Privacy reputation is best-in-class: German jurisdiction, AES-encrypted drives plus optional per-user crypto mail storage Posteo cannot reverse, no IP logging, anonymous cash payment, transparency reports since 2014, has litigated against overbroad data requests; no privacy incidents found in 2025-2026. Deliverability of personal mail is solid (long-standing conservative anti-abuse posture, no blacklist incidents surfaced), but Posteo is unusable as a creator sending platform: ToS bans commercial advertising and standardized mail to many recipients, with limits around 500 emails/hour and 1,000/day. Creator fit is weak — no own-domain identity, no newsletter tooling, utilitarian Roundcube-style webmail. Competitive read for Letters: Posteo wins the pure privacy-mailbox buyer at 1/8th of Letters' $8 mailbox price, but its principled refusal of custom domains means it cannot serve authors, newsletter writers, or small presses who need their own domain — exactly the gap Letters' $20/creator-domain tier targets; position Letters as "Posteo-grade privacy, but on your own domain and built for creators." TechRadar's May 2025 review echoes this: excellent security, very cheap, but limited by no custom domains and few features.

competitors.price: Entry: Light €1/mo (~$1.15, no custom domain). Custom domain gated at Standard: €3/mo (~$3.50 USD) with annual billing after the July 2026 increase (was €2.50); Premium €9/mo (~$10.50, was €7.50). No free tier (30-day trial only). Storage doubles Sept 1, 2026 (Standard 10→20 GB mail).
competitors.positioning: Berlin-based (Heinlein Group) privacy-first email + groupware suite selling GDPR-compliant, ad-free, PGP-capable mailboxes with cheap custom-domain support to privacy-conscious individuals and small businesses in German data centers.
competitors.notes: Active and growing, not defunct (operating since 2014). Summer 2026 plan change: prices up ~20% (new customers since Jul 15, 2026; existing from Aug 31, 2026) with mail/Drive storage doubled from Sep 1; Light tier unchanged. Custom domains work on Standard (€3/mo, 50 aliases + catch-all) and Premium (250 aliases) but setup is manual DNS with an external registrar — no registration service. Material security blemish: mailbox.org does not fully enforce SPF/DKIM/DMARC anti-spoofing for custom domains — community reports (2024-2025, unresolved) that any mailbox.org account can send as another user's custom-domain address; this triggered an ongoing "Remove Mailbox.org" debate on Privacy Guides, though it remains listed as recommended. Privacy strengths: Stiftung Warentest test winner ("Very Good" 1.4), no ads/tracking/data sharing, anonymous cash payment, eco-powered German servers; caveat: Guard PGP is server-side, not true E2EE (weaker than Proton/Tuta). Deliverability: solid outbound reputation, generous limits (10k mails/day private, though spam heuristics can block ~5k); criticisms center on the inbound spam filter, not blocklisting. Creator fit is weak: Open-Xchange webmail is groupware-oriented and dated (OX v8 migration drew complaints), no newsletter/audience tooling, and it is not an ESP — creators would still need a separate newsletter service. Vs Letters: undercuts $8/mailbox at €3/mo with a stronger privacy brand, but no indie-creator UX, no newsletter story, and the custom-domain spoofing gap is a direct wedge for a "your domain, done right" pitch.

providers.name: Amazon SES
providers.outbound: SES v2 API (SendEmail/SendRawEmail) or SMTP. Both directions supported, up to 40MB messages by default on v2. New accounts start in a sandbox (verified recipients only, 200 msgs/24h, 1 msg/sec) and must file a production-access request, typically reviewed in 24-48h (docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/request-production-access.html). Shared IP pool by default (generally decent reputation but you inherit neighbors and must maintain your own bounce/complaint metrics or risk account-level pausing); dedicated IPs optional at extra cost. Reputation management (warm-up, suppression, feedback loops) is largely on you compared with Postmark/Resend.
providers.inbound: Yes — true MX-based receiving, but only in specific regions (all receiving resources except S3 must be in the same region). You publish an MX record pointing at e.g. inbound-smtp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, then receipt rules deliver to S3, invoke Lambda, or publish to SNS; there is NO native 'POST JSON to my HTTPS webhook' — you build that glue (typical pattern: S3 + Lambda that parses raw MIME and POSTs to your Next.js route, since SNS-embedded email payloads are size-capped). Inbound size limit 40MB. Payload is raw RFC822 MIME — you parse it yourself (mailparser etc.). Optional Mail Manager adds richer ingress/routing at significant extra cost.
providers.pricing: $0.10 per 1,000 outbound emails ($0.0001/email) + $0.12/GB attachments; inbound $0.10 per 1,000 received emails (first 1,000/mo free) plus $0.10 per 1,000 256KB chunks. The old free tier (3,000 message charges/mo for 12 months) was discontinued for accounts created after ~July 2025; new accounts instead get $200 general AWS Free Tier credits. Mail Manager (optional): $50/mo per open ingress endpoint + $0.15/1k processed. Dedicated IP extra. Source: aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/ (page itself egress-blocked in this sandbox; figures corroborated by smtpedia.com/amazon-aws-ses-pricing/, costgoat.com/pricing/amazon-ses, freetier.co/directory/products/amazon-ses, all Aug 2026).
providers.custom_domain_model: Fully programmatic and multi-tenant-proven: sesv2 CreateEmailIdentity per creator domain returns 3 Easy DKIM tokens you render as CNAME records for the creator to add; SES auto-detects and flips the identity to verified (BYODKIM also supported by passing DkimSigningAttributes). GetEmailIdentity polls verification status. No per-domain fee and effectively unlimited identities — the classic SaaS pattern. Inbound for creator domains additionally requires each creator to point MX at your SES region endpoint. Docs: docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/APIReference-V2/API_CreateEmailIdentity.html.
providers.verdict: Best unit economics at scale and the only mainstream API vendor with unmetered-domains outbound + real inbound, but highest glue-code cost: you must build the S3/Lambda-to-webhook bridge, MIME parsing, signature verification, and your own suppression/reputation tooling, and pass production-access review with a 'user-generated newsletter' story (AWS scrutinizes multi-tenant senders). Strong candidate for the post-MVP cost-optimization step rather than the MVP itself.

providers.name: Resend
providers.outbound: Modern REST API (POST /emails), batch endpoint, React Email templates, idempotency keys; SMTP relay also available. Shared IPs by default with generally good deliverability reports; dedicated IPs reserved for Scale/Enterprise. Younger reputation track record than Postmark/SES but purpose-built for exactly this Next.js/Vercel developer profile — and Letters already has a Resend outbound adapter built (lib/mail), so it is the incumbent.
providers.inbound: YES — Inbound launched Nov 3, 2025 (resend.com/blog/inbound-emails), so any pre-Nov-2025 claim that 'Resend has no inbound' is stale. You add an MX record on a receiving domain (docs strongly recommend a subdomain, e.g. mail.creator.com, because the MX captures ALL mail for that name), then an `email.received` webhook (Svix-signed) POSTs JSON to your endpoint. Caveat per third-party comparisons: the webhook payload is comparatively thin — metadata (from, to, subject, attachment filenames) with full body/attachment content fetched via follow-up API calls (docs: resend.com/docs/dashboard/receiving/introduction). Feature is <1 year old — less battle-tested than Postmark/Mailgun inbound.
providers.pricing: Free: 3,000 emails/mo, 100/day. Pro: $20/mo for 50k (a $35 step for 100k). Scale: $90/mo for 100k up to $1,150 for 2.5M; overage ~$0.90/1k (pay-as-you-go added 2025). Important for Letters: received (inbound) emails count against the SAME quota as sent, one credit per email, and each To/Cc/Bcc recipient of an outbound send counts separately — a 5,000-subscriber newsletter issue consumes 5,000 credits. Source: resend.com/pricing (egress-blocked here; corroborated by flexprice.io/blog/detailed-resend-pricing-guide, resend.com/docs/knowledge-base/account-quotas-and-limits via search, Aug 2026).
providers.custom_domain_model: Programmatic: POST /domains returns the SPF + DKIM records (and now optional MX for receiving) to show the creator; GET /domains/{id} + verify endpoint to poll status — same UX shape as SES/Postmark. Domain caps are plan-gated: Free ~1-3 domains, Pro ~100, Scale 1,000 — so per-creator custom domains push you to Scale ($90/mo) as creator count grows. Webhooks are Svix-signed (svix signature verification).
providers.verdict: Best MVP fit and already integrated: one vendor, one API family, both directions, first-class Next.js/Vercel DX, and per-domain onboarding built for multi-tenant SaaS. Dealbreaker-watch items: recipient-count billing makes newsletter fan-out the dominant cost (2.5M sends = $1,150/mo vs $250 on SES), inbound counts against the same quota, the inbound payload requires follow-up API fetches for bodies, and Inbound is only ~10 months old. Recommended: keep Resend for MVP, keep the provider seam so SES can take over fan-out economics later.

providers.name: Postmark
providers.outbound: Transactional-focused API with separate Message Streams (transactional vs 'Broadcast' for newsletter-style bulk — Letters would need Broadcast streams). Reputation is the best-in-class story: consistently top published deliverability, strict content/approval vetting of new accounts, custom Return-Path support for SPF/DMARC alignment (postmarkapp.com/support/article/how-do-i-verify-a-domain). Owned by ActiveCampaign. The vetting that protects its IPs also means a multi-tenant user-generated-content sender gets extra scrutiny.
providers.inbound: The reference-quality inbound webhook: Postmark receives on an inbound address/domain (MX to inbound.postmarkapp.com), fully parses the message, and POSTs a single rich JSON document to your webhook — FromFull/ToFull/CcFull objects, Subject, TextBody, HtmlBody, StrippedTextReply, Headers array, and Attachments inline as base64 with Name/ContentType/ContentLength (postmarkapp.com/developer/webhooks/inbound-webhook). No follow-up API calls needed; ideal shape for a Supabase-backed Next.js route. Inbound processing is gated to Pro/Platform tiers in the 2025+ pricing model.
providers.pricing: 2025/2026 tiered model: Free/dev tier (100 emails/mo), Basic $15/mo per 10k, Pro $16.50/mo per 10k (adds inbound processing; overage ~$1.30/1k), Platform $18/mo per 10k. No separate webhook fees. This per-10k block pricing is ~13-18x SES per email and scales poorly for newsletter volume. Source: postmarkapp.com/pricing (egress-blocked here; corroborated by costbench.com/software/email-api/postmark/, sequenzy.com/pricing/postmark, klymentiev.com/blog/postmark-pricing, Aug 2026).
providers.custom_domain_model: Full Domains API: POST /domains creates a sender domain and returns DKIMPendingHost/DKIMPendingTextValue (TXT record) plus custom Return-Path CNAME to hand to the creator; verification auto-detects within ~48h with a manual verify endpoint (postmarkapp.com/developer/api/domains-api, postmarkapp.com/support/article/1113-how-do-i-manage-domains-using-the-api). Inbound domains configured per-server with MX. Multi-tenant 'servers' concept maps well to per-creator isolation on the Platform tier.
providers.verdict: Best-in-class inbound payload and deliverability, and a clean domains API — but two MVP frictions: inbound requires the Pro tier and per-10k pricing makes creator newsletter fan-out expensive fast, and its strict transactional vetting is an awkward fit for a platform sending other people's newsletters. Strong as an inbound-only or transactional-only sidecar; weak as the sole MTA for Letters' economics.

providers.name: Mailgun
providers.outbound: Mature send API (v3 messages, v4 domains) + SMTP; EU and US regions (relevant for privacy-first positioning). Deliverability reputation is middling-to-good: shared IP pools vary by plan tier (cheaper plans share with rougher cohorts), dedicated IPs on higher plans; Sinch-owned. Flex pay-as-you-go price doubled to ~$2/1k in Dec 2025, signaling upmarket pressure.
providers.inbound: Yes — the oldest-established 'inbound routes' product. You point creator-domain MX at mxa/mxb.mailgun.org, create a Route via API (match_recipient expression → forward(https://yourapp.com/api/inbound)), and Mailgun POSTs a fully parsed message as application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data: body-plain, body-html, stripped-text, stripped-html (quotes/signatures removed), message-headers JSON, attachments (documentation.mailgun.com/docs/mailgun/user-manual/receive-forward-store/receive-http). Requests carry timestamp+token+signature verified with HMAC-SHA256 over your signing key. Store-and-notify variant keeps the message 3 days for retrieval. Form-encoded (not JSON) payload is slightly clunkier in a Next.js route but well-trodden.
providers.pricing: Free: 100 emails/day, 1 custom domain, 1 inbound route. Basic $15/mo (1 domain, 5 routes). Foundation $35/mo: 50k emails, 1,000 custom domains, full inbound routing. Scale $90/mo adds SSO, dedicated IP options, longer retention. Flex PAYG ~$2/1k after Dec 2025 repricing. Inbound received messages count toward plan volume. Source: mailgun.com/pricing/ (egress-blocked here; corroborated by costbench.com/software/email-api/mailgun/, usebouncer.com/mailgun-pricing/, saaspricepulse.com/tools/mailgun, Aug 2026).
providers.custom_domain_model: Programmatic and explicitly multi-tenant: POST /v4/domains creates a sending domain and returns sending_dns_records (SPF TXT + DKIM, or CNAME-based 'Automatic Sender Security' DKIM where Mailgun rotates keys) plus receiving MX records; PUT verify endpoint re-checks DNS (documentation.mailgun.com/docs/mailgun/api-reference/send/mailgun/domains/post-v4-domains). 1,000 domains included at Foundation — the best domains-per-dollar of the commercial APIs. Routes are account-wide and match on recipient expressions, so one wildcard route can serve all creator domains.
providers.verdict: The most complete single-vendor feature match for Letters (outbound + parsed inbound webhooks + 1,000 domains at $35/mo), and the only one with CNAME-delegated auto-rotating DKIM. Trade-offs: deliverability reputation a notch below Postmark/SES-with-care, form-encoded inbound payload, recent aggressive repricing, and Sinch ownership sits oddly with a privacy-first brand. Solid runner-up to Resend for MVP; arguably ahead of it once inbound volume matters.

providers.name: Cloudflare Email Routing (+ new Email Service)
providers.outbound: Historically none (Email Routing only forwards/replies). This changed: Cloudflare Email Sending entered public beta April 16, 2026 under the merged 'Cloudflare Email Service' — send via Workers binding env.EMAIL.send(), REST API, or SMTP, with HTML/attachments (blog.cloudflare.com/email-for-agents/, developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-04-16-email-sending-public-beta/). Beta-grade, agent/transactional-oriented; no published multi-tenant custom-domain sending story or deliverability track record yet. Requires Workers Paid ($5/mo).
providers.inbound: Yes, with the key constraint CONFIRMED: Email Routing only works on zones served by Cloudflare's nameservers — the MX/SPF/DKIM records it manages live in your Cloudflare DNS zone (developers.cloudflare.com/email-routing/setup/email-routing-dns-records/). And YES, it can route to a Worker: a routing rule's 'Send to a Worker' action invokes an email handler receiving ForwardableEmailMessage (from, to, headers, raw as ReadableStream, rawSize); the Worker can parse with postal-mime and fetch() a POST to any HTTPS webhook — e.g. your Vercel /api/inbound route (developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/api/route-emails/email-handler/). You build the payload format yourself; Worker failures surface only as 'dropped' in stats. Limits: 200 rules/200 destination addresses per zone; ~25 MiB message cap; Workers CPU/memory limits apply to parsing.
providers.pricing: Email Routing (inbound/forwarding + Email Workers): free — unlimited custom addresses, no per-message charge. Email Sending beta: 3,000 messages/account/mo included, then $0.35/1k, on Workers Paid $5/mo. Sources: developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/ and blog.cloudflare.com/email-for-agents/ (both egress-blocked here; figures via search results from those pages plus community.cloudflare.com mirror, Apr-Aug 2026).
providers.custom_domain_model: The dealbreaker for multi-tenant: there is no API to attach an external creator domain — each domain must be a full zone in a Cloudflare account with Cloudflare nameservers. Per-creator custom domains would force every creator to delegate their entire DNS to your Cloudflare account (or run their own CF account + Worker), unlike SES/Resend/Postmark/Mailgun where creators just paste 2-4 records. Cloudflare-for-SaaS custom hostnames do NOT extend to Email Routing. Fine for domains YOU own (letters.app inbound at $0).
providers.verdict: Not viable as the per-creator-domain MTA: the Cloudflare-nameserver requirement breaks the 'creator keeps their DNS, adds a few records' onboarding model, and outbound sending is a months-old beta with no reputation history. Excellent, though, as a free inbound tap for Letters' OWN domains (support@, reply-to relays) via Worker→webhook, and worth rechecking Email Service once sending GA's.

providers.name: Postal (self-hosted)
providers.outbound: Full open-source mail delivery platform (MIT, Ruby): HTTP send API + SMTP, per-organization mail servers, built-in queueing, click/open tracking, and a web UI. Deliverability is entirely yours: dedicated non-blocklisted IPs, correct PTR/rDNS, and 2-4 weeks of IP warm-up starting at a few hundred msgs/day before real volume; every inbox-provider relationship, FBL, and blocklist delisting is your job (pinkyspy.com/en/posts/postal-mail-server/, learnwithhasan.com/guide/self-host-postal-smtp/).
providers.inbound: Yes, natively closest to what Letters wants from self-hosting: Postal accepts inbound SMTP for your domains and can deliver each message to an HTTP endpoint (webhook-style POST with parsed message) as well as forwarding. So the SES-style glue layer is built in — but the SMTP edge, spam filtering (SpamAssassin/rspamd integration), and TLS are yours to run.
providers.pricing: Software free (MIT). Real cost is infra + ops: a Linux host or k8s cluster, MariaDB/MySQL (one DB per provisioned mail server), Docker Compose or Helm; historical RabbitMQ dependency removed in v3. Realistic floor ~$20-60/mo VPS + dedicated IP(s), plus the port-25-unblock dance with the host, plus meaningful ongoing engineer time. Sources: openapps.pro/apps/postal, pinkyspy.com/en/posts/postal-mail-server/ (docs.postalserver.io egress-blocked here).
providers.custom_domain_model: Good for self-hosted: Postal manages per-domain DKIM keys, SPF and return-path records itself and exposes them per domain (API + UI), so a creator-onboarding flow (create domain → show records → poll verification) is buildable. But YOU are the DKIM signer and the MX target, so every creator domain's deliverability rides on your IP pool's reputation with zero vendor cushion.
providers.verdict: Feature-wise the best self-hosted match (both directions, HTTP API, per-domain DKIM, inbound-to-webhook built in), and philosophically aligned with privacy-first (no third party sees mail). But ops burden is moderate-to-high and architecturally opposed to the Vercel/Supabase serverless posture — a stateful Ruby/MariaDB mail cluster with IP-warming on-call is a company function, not an MVP feature. Revisit at the 'own the infrastructure' stage, not now.

providers.name: Postfix / Haraka (raw self-hosted MTAs)
providers.outbound: Postfix: the most widely deployed OSS MTA, battle-proven at massive scale, C + config files; DKIM signing needs OpenDKIM/rspamd bolted on. Haraka: event-driven Node.js SMTP server with a JS plugin architecture — attractive to a JS team for custom delivery logic (haraka.github.io, github.com/haraka/Haraka). Both give you zero reputation head start: your IPs, your warm-up, your blocklist appeals; most clouds (and Hetzner et al.) block outbound port 25 until you request unblocking — and you cannot run any of this on Vercel at all; it needs an always-on VPS/box.
providers.inbound: Both can receive: Haraka is explicitly strong as an inbound edge with anti-spam plugins and is well-suited to a custom 'accept SMTP → parse → POST JSON to webhook' plugin (its plugin model makes this a few hundred lines); Postfix would typically pipe to a script or LMTP consumer that you write. Neither is a mail store or provides any webhook/payload format out of the box — the entire parsed-JSON contract (like Postmark's) is yours to design, plus SPF/DKIM/DMARC validation, spam scoring, and retry semantics.
providers.pricing: Software free (GPL/MIT-style). Cost = VPS with clean dedicated IP(s) (~$10-50/mo), reverse DNS, monitoring, and substantial engineering time; no vendor pricing page applies. Sources: haraka.github.io/getting_started/, reviewmyemails.com/emailalmanac/esp-and-infrastructure/providers-esp-smtp-mta/popular-self-hosted-mtas, iaziz786.com/blog/self-hosted-smtp-haraka/.
providers.custom_domain_model: Entirely DIY: no domains API, no DKIM-record vending. You'd generate per-creator DKIM keypairs, publish selectors, template the records for creators, wire per-domain signing into OpenDKIM/Haraka's dkim_sign plugin, and build verification polling — i.e., re-implement the SES/Resend/Mailgun onboarding product from scratch before writing any Letters feature.
providers.verdict: Not an MVP option. Strictly dominated by Postal for self-hosting (Postal is roughly 'Haraka/Postfix + the domains API + inbound webhooks + UI you would otherwise build'). The only future niche: Haraka as a custom inbound-only edge (no sending reputation needed for receiving, and inbound port 25 is not blocked) if Letters later wants a privacy-preserving in-house MX in front of its webhook while keeping a commercial provider for outbound.

compliance.gmail_yahoo_bulk_requirements: BASELINE (took effect Feb 1, 2024; Google + Yahoo jointly): senders of >=5,000 messages/day to Gmail or Yahoo consumer inboxes are "bulk senders" (Google counts 5k/day to Gmail across all mail streams from the same primary From: domain; once a bulk sender, always treated as one). Requirements: (1) AUTHENTICATION - SPF *and* DKIM must both pass, plus a DMARC record on the From: domain (minimum p=none), and the message must pass DMARC alignment: the From: header domain must align (relaxed alignment OK, i.e. subdomain match) with the SPF domain (MAIL FROM/Return-Path) or the DKIM d= domain. All senders (any volume) need at least SPF or DKIM, valid forward+reverse DNS (PTR) on sending IPs, and TLS for transmission. (2) ONE-CLICK UNSUBSCRIBE - RFC 8058 List-Unsubscribe + List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click headers required on marketing/promotional bulk mail (deadline was June 1, 2024); Google requires the unsubscribe POST to be honored within 2 days; a visible unsubscribe link in the body is also required; transactional mail is exempt. (3) SPAM COMPLAINT RATE - keep the user-reported spam rate in Google Postmaster Tools below 0.1%, and NEVER at/above 0.3%; Yahoo uses the same 0.3% ceiling via its Complaint Feedback Loop. Sustained >=0.3% causes filtering/rejection, and mitigation eligibility requires staying under 0.3% for ~7 consecutive days. UPDATES SINCE FEB 2024: enforcement was phased (temporary errors on a % of non-compliant traffic from April 2024, escalating); in 2025 Google moved from Postmaster Tools warnings to SMTP-level enforcement - as of November 2025 non-compliant bulk mail gets temporary (4xx) and permanent (5xx) rejections rather than junk-foldering. Also relevant since then: Microsoft Outlook.com (outlook.com/hotmail/live) adopted matching rules for >5,000/day senders effective May 5, 2025 (SPF+DKIM+DMARC p=none with alignment; non-compliant mail rejected with 550 5.7.15; functional From/Reply-To, visible unsubscribe, list hygiene). PLATFORM IMPLICATION for a host of per-creator domains: each creator's From: domain needs its own DKIM signature and DMARC record aligned to that domain (mail DKIM-signed only by the relay's domain, e.g. d=amazonses.com, fails alignment); the platform should inject RFC 8058 headers and process one-click POSTs automatically for every creator, and monitor per-domain spam rates via Google Postmaster Tools v2 API and Yahoo Complaint Feedback Loop. Note the thresholds are per From: domain, so small creators may be under 5k/day individually - but Google explicitly recommends all senders comply, and the relay providers (SES/Resend) contractually require it regardless of volume.
compliance.can_spam: CAN-SPAM (15 U.S.C. 7701-7713; FTC CAN-SPAM Rule, 16 CFR Part 316) puts nearly all obligations on the "sender" and "initiator" of a commercial message - here, the CREATOR: (a) no false/misleading header info (From, Reply-To, routing must identify the person who initiated); (b) no deceptive subject lines; (c) identify the message as an ad; (d) include the sender's valid physical postal address; (e) provide a clear opt-out mechanism that works for at least 30 days after sending; (f) honor opt-outs within 10 business days, with no fee/login required; (g) no sending to opted-out addresses and no selling/transferring those addresses. Penalties are per-email, up to $53,088 per violation (2025 FTC inflation-adjusted figure). THE PLATFORM (host/relay) is generally NOT an initiator thanks to the "routine conveyance" exemption: 15 U.S.C. 7702(15) defines routine conveyance as transmission/routing/relaying/handling/storing, through an automatic technical process, of a message for which ANOTHER person identified the recipients or supplied the addresses - and 7702(9) excludes routine conveyance from "initiate". So a host whose creators upload their own lists and hit send is not the CAN-SPAM sender for that mail. BUT the shield is lost where the platform goes beyond conveyance: "procure" (7702(12)) includes intentionally paying or inducing another to send, and liability attaches if the platform selects recipients, appends its own commercial content that promotes the platform's products (that can make the platform a "sender" for its portion), or knowingly assists violative campaigns; FTC guidance also stresses that liability is joint - more than one person may be an initiator, and none of it can be contracted away. PRACTICAL PLATFORM OBLIGATIONS: (1) don't alter headers in ways that make them misleading; (2) ToS requiring CAN-SPAM compliance (address block, opt-out honoring, no harvested/dictionary-attack lists - those are "aggravated violations" under 7704(b)); (3) enforce a global per-creator suppression list so opt-outs are honored within 10 business days even if the creator is inactive; (4) require the physical-address footer in templates; (5) note the platform, as a provider of an "Internet access service", also has standing under 7706(g) to sue spammers abusing it. If the platform ever sends its own promotional mail to creators or subscribers, it is fully a CAN-SPAM sender for those messages.
compliance.spf_dkim_dmarc_plan: Per creator domain creator.com, sending From: e.g. hello@creator.com via a relay. Key principle: DMARC alignment comes from DKIM d=creator.com (robust, survives forwarding) plus SPF on a custom bounce/MAIL FROM subdomain of creator.com (SPF is evaluated on the envelope MAIL FROM domain, not the From: header, so an SPF include on the root apex does nothing for DMARC unless MAIL FROM uses the creator's domain). PLAN A - AMAZON SES (Easy DKIM + custom MAIL FROM): (1) DKIM/verification - 3 CNAMEs: {token1|2|3}._domainkey.creator.com -> {token}.dkim.amazonses.com (serves as both domain verification and DKIM signing with d=creator.com; SES auto-rotates keys ~every 90 days; use 2048-bit). (2) Custom MAIL FROM subdomain, e.g. bounce.creator.com, configured on the SES identity: MX bounce.creator.com -> 10 feedback-smtp.<region>.amazonses.com, and TXT bounce.creator.com -> "v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all". This yields SPF pass + relaxed DMARC alignment (bounce.creator.com is a subdomain of the From: domain). Without it the envelope sender is amazonses.com and SPF never aligns - the #1 SES DMARC failure. (3) DMARC - TXT _dmarc.creator.com -> "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@reports.yourplatform.com; fo=1" (point rua at a platform-controlled aggregate-report mailbox/monitoring service so you watch all creators centrally; an external rua destination needs the verification TXT creator.com._report._dmarc.reports.yourplatform.com -> "v=DMARC1"). Start p=none, move to p=quarantine then p=reject per domain once reports show only aligned mail. Keep default relaxed alignment (aspf=r, adkim=r) so the subdomain MAIL FROM aligns. PLAN B - RESEND: Resend puts records on a send subdomain by default: (1) MX send.creator.com -> feedback-smtp.<region>.amazonses.com priority 10 (bounce handling; Resend rides SES infra); (2) TXT send.creator.com -> "v=spf1 include:_spf.resend.com ~all" (exact value from dashboard); (3) DKIM TXT resend._domainkey.creator.com -> "p=<public key from dashboard>" (signs d=creator.com); (4) same _dmarc.creator.com record as above. OPERATIONAL NOTES for the platform: generate these records per creator via the SES/Resend API and show them as a copy-paste table (or offer delegated subdomains / CNAME-based setup to minimize creator error); poll verification (SES GetIdentityVerificationAttributes / Resend verify endpoint) and block sending until DKIM + MAIL FROM/SPF + DMARC all verify; re-check periodically since creators break DNS; never share one DKIM key across creators; add the RFC 8058 List-Unsubscribe/List-Unsubscribe-Post headers at the relay layer. If a creator's From: is on a subdomain (news.creator.com), publish DMARC at the org domain or that subdomain and keep MAIL FROM under the same org domain for relaxed alignment.
compliance.pii_retention: ROLE SPLIT drives everything. Under GDPR the platform is a PROCESSOR (Art. 28) for creators' subscriber PII and stored message content (the creator is controller), and a CONTROLLER for its own account data (creator emails, billing, logs). Under CCPA/CPRA the platform is a SERVICE PROVIDER for creator data and a BUSINESS for its own. GDPR obligations: (1) Art. 28 DPA with every creator covering processing scope, subprocessors (AWS SES/Resend/Supabase/Vercel must be listed and flowed down), security, and - critically - Art. 28(3)(g): delete or return all personal data at the end of services and delete existing copies; (2) storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)): keep identifiable data no longer than necessary - adopt and document a retention schedule per data class (message bodies, recipient lists, send/bounce logs, suppression entries); suppression lists can be retained as a legal-obligation/legitimate-interest carve-out since they exist to honor opt-outs; (3) Art. 17 erasure: when a subscriber's request reaches the creator (or the platform directly - a processor must forward it and assist per Art. 28(3)(e)), delete from live mailboxes/DB "without undue delay" - controller must respond within one month (Art. 12(3)); (4) backups: regulators accept that immutable backups need not be purged instantly - put the data "beyond use" (excluded from restore/re-processing) and let it age out in the normal backup rotation, documenting the cycle length; (5) Art. 33 breach notification to the controller without undue delay (controller has 72h to its authority). CCPA/CPRA obligations: (1) as a service provider, delete consumer PI on the business's (creator's) instruction and flow deletion down to subprocessors; contract must restrict use to the contracted services; (2) as a business (for creator account data), acknowledge deletion requests within 10 business days and complete within 45 calendar days (+45-day extension with notice); (3) CPRA retention rules: disclose, per category of PI, the retention period or the criteria used to determine it, and do not retain PI longer than reasonably necessary for the disclosed purpose; (4) archived/backup systems may defer deletion until the backup is restored or accessed/used. CONCRETE DESIGN FOR AN EMAIL HOST: retention schedule such as message content retained while the account is active + N days after cancellation (e.g. 30-90) then hard-deleted; SMTP/send logs 30-90 days; bounce/complaint events 12-24 months (deliverability legitimate interest); suppression/opt-out list retained indefinitely (hashed if possible) as a compliance record; deletion API that cascades to relay stores (note SES/Resend keep their own short-lived content/event data - cover them in the subprocessor list); tombstone-and-rotate approach for backups; per-creator export (return of data) at offboarding.
